newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Mining at Carrick several yrs away - Summit.
newsitem.headline: Mining at Carrick several yrs away - Summit.

text.p: Summit Gold NL chairman Colin Beyer said on Friday that tests confirming the presence of gold at the Carrick goldfield in Central Otago in New Zealand's South Island were extremely encouraging, but any mining was several years away.

"We'll probably have to do a lot more drilling to identify the extent of the occurrence, and I would say it would be a year of two away before a goldmine could be established after we'd got to the stage of having identified an economic resource," Beyer told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"So it's early days, but what we've got is extremely encouraging."

Earlier, Summit said a secondary phase of soil sampling, combined with previously reported soil results, had clearly defined a strong coincident gold arsenic hanging wall anomaly averaging 150 metres wide, and a second narrow 20 to 40 metre wide footwall zone to the west.
The sampling showed gold values up to 2.75 grams per tonne in the zones which extended for over two kilometres.

"That's in the soil sample, so we would expect that we'd be looking at something with a better value than that," Beyer said. "If the deposit's large enough, it becomes extremely economic...but who knows, we might be disappointed."
Percussion drilling was scheduled to start at Carrick in the first quarter of 1997.
Beyer said Summit was the sole owner of the tenement after several unsuccessful partnerships.
"We've had a couple of joint venture partners, but frankly we didn't agree in the end with the way in which they were approaching the mineralisation," he said.
"In the end we decided to do it ourselves because we've been able to conserve our money pretty well and we were able to afford to drill it ourselves."
He said Carrick had very similar features to the nearby mineralisation at Macraes Mining in North Otago and was in the same schist belt.
"The fact is that one never looks for gold in places where it's never occurred before and Carrick is covered with old small goldmines."

The company had systematically gone over the area and identified with reasonable precision where the mineralisation came from. "It comes from molten rock which has been permeated by superheated water for million of years," said Beyer.
He said the company would be keeping shareholders and the investing public well in touch with developments.

"We've also got another very good project in Australia with the uranium of course, so it's a matter of establishing priorities and I guess that depends on where the value of these minerals is going," he said.
In December Summit said drilling results from its Valhalla project in northwest Queensland had revealed wide zones of uranium mineralisation.

When Summit first reported finding traces of gold at Carrick and uranium at Valhalla in mid-December, its share price spiked up sharply to a peak of 85 NZ cents before easing back to 60 cents. A year ago the share price was around seven cents.
The miner's stock rose eight cents today after news of the secondary Carrick tests was released. It eased to 60 NZ cents in afternoon trade, up six.

Summit, which has never posted a profit, is a New Zealand corporation listed in New Zealand and Australia and is about 34 percent owned by directors following a management buyout early in 1996. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
